fathers/athanasius/summary: Athanasius (c. 296–373), deacon at Nicaea and bishop of Alexandria for 45 years, five times exiled, made the Nicene ‘one in being’ (homoousios) the rallying point against Arianism, wrote the classic On the Incarnation and the Life of Antony, and in his 39th Festal Letter (367) gave the first list of exactly the 27 New Testament books.
fathers/athanasius/story:
Athanasius was born in or near Alexandria around 296–298 and educated within the church. As deacon and secretary to Bishop Alexander, he attended the Council of Nicaea (325), which condemned Arius’ teaching that the Son was a creature with a beginning. In 328 he succeeded Alexander as bishop, despite claims that he was under canonical age, and immediately faced opposition from Melitian schismatics and from the pro-Arian circle around Eusebius of Nicomedia.

His episcopate became a struggle with emperors and councils. He was exiled by Constantine to Trier (335–337) after the Council of Tyre accused him of violence; by Constantius II to Rome (339–346), where he gained the support of Julius I and the West; to the Egyptian desert (356–362) after soldiers broke into his church; by Julian (362–363); and briefly by Valens (365–366). The monks of Egypt sheltered him, and the phrase ‘Athanasius against the world’ (Athanasius contra mundum) captures his later legend.

His early double work Against the Pagans–On the Incarnation (probably 330s) argues that the Word through whom the world was made became human to restore the image of God and to defeat death: ‘He became human that we might become divine’ (On the Incarnation 54). In the Orations against the Arians (c. 339–345) and On the Decrees of Nicaea he defended homoousios — a non-scriptural word he initially used sparingly — on the grounds that only one who is truly God can save and deify, and that worshipping a creature would be idolatry. In his Letters to Serapion (c. 359) he extended the argument to the full divinity of the Holy Spirit.

At the Council of Alexandria (362) he helped reconcile those who spoke of ‘one hypostasis’ and ‘three hypostases’, opening the way to the Cappadocian settlement ratified at Constantinople in 381, eight years after his death. His Life of Antony (c. 357), presenting the desert hermit as an unlettered man taught by God and loyal to the bishops against Arians, became a bestseller in Latin translation; it helped spread monasticism to the West and played a part in Augustine’s conversion (Confessions 8.6).

His 39th Festal Letter (Easter 367) lists the 27 books of the New Testament as ‘springs of salvation’, with the Hebrew canon (plus Baruch) for the Old Testament and books such as the Didache and Shepherd of Hermas recommended for catechumens but not canonical. Modern historians (notably R. P. C. Hanson, Timothy Barnes and David Gwynn) have portrayed his use of force and polemic more critically, and stressed that the ‘Arian’ party he attacked was less unified than his writings suggest.
fathers/athanasius/roots/0/text: Inherits the Alexandrian Logos theology of Origen while rejecting Origenist subordinationism; also echoes Irenaeus’ themes of recapitulation and divinisation.
fathers/athanasius/roots/1/text: Argues largely from scripture (John 1, Proverbs 8:22, Philippians 2) and treats the creature–Creator distinction of Genesis as decisive.
fathers/athanasius/roots/2/text: Uses Platonic categories of participation and image, but sharpens the Creator–creature divide in a way that breaks with the Platonic chain of being.
fathers/athanasius/roots/3/text: Closely allied to the Egyptian monks (Antony, Pachomius), who supported him in exile and whom he presented as models of Nicene orthodoxy.
fathers/athanasius/roots/4/text: His career was shaped throughout by imperial intervention after Constantine, from Nicaea to repeated exiles.
fathers/athanasius/keyTeachings/0: The Son is ‘one in being’ (homoousios) with the Father, true God from true God
fathers/athanasius/keyTeachings/1: The Word became flesh to restore the image of God and to conquer death and corruption
fathers/athanasius/keyTeachings/2: ‘He became human that we might become divine’ (theosis)
fathers/athanasius/keyTeachings/3: Only God can save; a created Son could not deify us
fathers/athanasius/keyTeachings/4: The Holy Spirit is fully divine, not a creature (Letters to Serapion)
fathers/athanasius/works/0/title: On the Incarnation of the Word (De Incarnatione)
fathers/athanasius/works/0/note: With Against the Pagans, a classic account of creation, fall and redemption.
fathers/athanasius/works/1/note: Main defence of the Son’s eternal divinity; the third Oration’s authenticity has been questioned.
fathers/athanasius/works/2/note: Founding hagiography of monasticism; translated into Latin by Evagrius of Antioch.
fathers/athanasius/works/3/note: First list of exactly the 27 New Testament books.
fathers/athanasius/works/4/title: Letters to Serapion on the Holy Spirit
fathers/athanasius/works/4/note: First major treatise on the divinity of the Spirit.
fathers/athanasius/works/5/title: History of the Arians and Apologia against the Arians
fathers/athanasius/works/5/note: Polemical histories with documents of the controversy.
fathers/athanasius/doctrineContributions: Made homoousios the touchstone of orthodoxy and argued for the Spirit’s divinity, preparing the creed of 381.
A Word–flesh Christology in which the divine Word is the subject of the incarnate life, a foundation for Cyril of Alexandria.
Classic formulation of salvation as deification and victory over death.
The 39th Festal Letter is the earliest list matching the present 27-book New Testament.
The Life of Antony shaped the ideal of the monk throughout East and West.
fathers/athanasius/laterInfluence/0/text: Basil sought his support, and his theology of homoousios and the Spirit fed directly into the Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed.
fathers/athanasius/laterInfluence/1/text: Cyril appealed to Athanasius (including works later shown to be Apollinarian forgeries) for ‘one incarnate nature of the Word’.
fathers/athanasius/laterInfluence/2/text: The Latin Life of Antony inspired Martin of Tours, Jerome and Augustine’s circle.
fathers/athanasius/laterInfluence/3/text: The Latin Quicunque vult (5th–6th century, probably southern Gaul) was attributed to him, though he did not write it; it was used by Catholics, Lutherans and Anglicans.
fathers/athanasius/laterInfluence/4/text: C. S. Lewis’ introduction to On the Incarnation (1944) popularised him; Thomas F. Torrance made him central to Reformed theology.
fathers/athanasius/reception/0/text: Saint and one of the four great Eastern Doctors of the Church (declared 1568); feast 2 May.
fathers/athanasius/reception/1/text: Called ‘the Great’ and ‘pillar of Orthodoxy’; commemorated 18 January (with Cyril) and 2 May.
fathers/athanasius/reception/2/text: The 20th Pope of Alexandria, called ‘the Apostolic’; central to Coptic identity and Christology.
fathers/athanasius/reception/3/text: Commemorated on 2 May; the Athanasian Creed attributed to him appears in the Book of Concord and the Book of Common Prayer.
fathers/athanasius/reception/4/text: Seen as the architect of an imposed orthodoxy and criticised for coercion and polemical distortion of opponents.
fathers/athanasius/controversies/0: Arian controversy and the five exiles
fathers/athanasius/controversies/1: Charges of violence against Melitians at the Council of Tyre (335)
fathers/athanasius/controversies/2: His polemical construction of a unified ‘Arian’ party
fathers/athanasius/controversies/3: Authenticity of Orations against the Arians III
fathers/athanasius/controversies/4: Relation to Marcellus of Ancyra, whom he long supported
fathers/athanasius/quote/text: He was made man that we might be made God.
fathers/ephrem-the-syrian/summary: Ephrem (c. 306–373), deacon of Nisibis and Edessa, is the greatest poet of early Christianity and the classic voice of a Semitic, non-Hellenised theology, teaching through symbol and paradox in hundreds of hymns (madrashe) sung by women’s choirs, against Arians, Marcionites, Bardaisan and Mani.
fathers/ephrem-the-syrian/story:
Ephrem was born around 306 in or near Nisibis (modern Nusaybin), then a Roman frontier fortress facing Persia. Later Greek and Syriac lives describing a pagan priest father and wild youth are legendary; his own writings suggest he grew up in a Christian family. He served Bishop Jacob of Nisibis and his successors as a deacon and teacher, and belonged to the ascetic ‘sons and daughters of the covenant’ (bnay qyama) who lived celibate lives within the church rather than as hermits.

He lived through the Persian sieges of Nisibis (338, 346, 350), which his Hymns on Nisibis (Carmina Nisibena) commemorate. When Jovian surrendered the city to Shapur II after Julian’s failed Persian campaign (363), its Christian population was evacuated and Ephrem settled in Edessa. There he taught, wrote and, according to tradition, organised relief during a famine shortly before his death on 9 June 373.

Ephrem wrote in Syriac, the Aramaic dialect of Edessa, in two main forms: the madrasha (teaching hymn) with stanzas and refrain, sung by choirs of consecrated women, and the memra (verse homily). Over 400 hymns survive, including the Hymns on Faith, On the Church, On Paradise, On the Nativity, On Virginity and the Unleavened Bread, along with a prose Commentary on the Diatessaron. The Greek ‘Ephraem Graecus’ corpus, very popular in Byzantium, is largely not by him.

His theology is poetic and symbolic rather than philosophical. God is hidden and revealed: he has ‘put on names’ and clothed himself in human language and in nature and scripture, which are two witnesses filled with ‘symbols’ (raze, ‘mysteries’) pointing to Christ. Against Arian ‘investigators’ who tried to define the Son, Ephrem attacked prying (‘bsatta’) into what can only be adored, while affirming Nicene faith. His hymns use vivid feminine and nuptial imagery, celebrate Mary as the new Eve and second ‘womb’ of the Word, and present the church and Paradise as a garden.

His writing also reflects the conflicts of his city: he argued against Marcionites, the followers of Bardaisan and Mani, and wrote sharply anti-Jewish polemic, reflecting rivalry with an influential Jewish community, that modern readers find troubling. Pope Benedict XV declared him a Doctor of the Church in 1920, and he is revered by Syriac Orthodox, Church of the East, Maronite and Byzantine traditions alike.
fathers/ephrem-the-syrian/roots/0/text: His Commentary on Genesis and hymns stay close to Semitic and Jewish interpretation of the Hebrew Bible, often paralleling targumic and rabbinic traditions.
fathers/ephrem-the-syrian/roots/1/text: Syriac Christianity grew in an Aramaic-speaking milieu close to Judaism; Ephrem shares Jewish exegetical traditions while polemicising against the synagogue.
fathers/ephrem-the-syrian/roots/2/text: Draws on the Edessene tradition of Addai and the Diatessaron, Tatian’s Gospel harmony, the standard Syriac Gospel text of his day.
fathers/ephrem-the-syrian/roots/3/text: His Prose Refutations and Hymns against Heresies attack Marcion, Bardaisan and Mani, defending the goodness of creation and the body.
fathers/ephrem-the-syrian/roots/4/text: Stands in the tradition of Jacob of Nisibis and of Aphrahat, the Persian Sage, with whom he shares the ascetic covenanter ideal.
fathers/ephrem-the-syrian/roots/5/text: Largely untouched by Greek philosophy, he nevertheless knows and rejects Greek ‘wisdom’ and Bardaisan’s Hellenistic cosmology.
fathers/ephrem-the-syrian/keyTeachings/0: God is known through symbols (raze) in nature and scripture, not by philosophical definition
fathers/ephrem-the-syrian/keyTeachings/1: Faith adores the mystery; ‘prying’ investigation into the Son’s generation is impiety
fathers/ephrem-the-syrian/keyTeachings/2: God ‘put on names’ and the Word ‘put on the body’: divine condescension through language and incarnation
fathers/ephrem-the-syrian/keyTeachings/3: Mary as the new Eve, holy and virgin, through whom the Word entered the world
fathers/ephrem-the-syrian/keyTeachings/4: The church as Paradise regained and the Eucharist as the fire and Spirit received in the bread
fathers/ephrem-the-syrian/keyTeachings/5: Goodness of creation and the body against Marcion, Bardaisan and Mani
fathers/ephrem-the-syrian/works/0/note: 87 madrashe against ‘investigators’ of the Son; key Nicene witness in Syriac.
fathers/ephrem-the-syrian/works/1/note: 15 hymns on Eden, the church and the soul.
fathers/ephrem-the-syrian/works/2/note: Christmas and Epiphany hymns rich in Marian imagery.
fathers/ephrem-the-syrian/works/3/note: Hymns on the sieges and bishops of Nisibis and on death and Satan.
fathers/ephrem-the-syrian/works/4/note: Prose commentary on Tatian’s Gospel harmony, preserved in Syriac and Armenian.
fathers/ephrem-the-syrian/doctrineContri: The classic exponent of a Semitic, symbolic theology distinct from Greek and Latin modes.
Shaped Syriac liturgical poetry and hymn-singing, including women’s choirs.
Rich early Marian theology later used in Syriac, Byzantine and Latin devotion.
Defended Nicene faith in Syriac through poetry rather than technical vocabulary.
His penitential and ascetic spirituality became popular through Greek and later Slavonic translations.
fathers/ephrem-the-syrian/laterInfluence: His hymns remain central to the liturgies of the Syriac Orthodox, Maronite, Assyrian and Malankara churches.
His madrasha form likely influenced the kontakion of Romanos the Melodist (6th century), himself from Syria.
The Lenten ‘Prayer of St Ephrem’ (‘O Lord and Master of my life…’) is said throughout Byzantine Lent.
Sebastian Brock and Sidney Griffith presented him as a model of non-Western, poetic and ecological theology.
fathers/ephrem-the-syrian/reception/0/tr: Syriac Orthodox and Church of the East
fathers/ephrem-the-syrian/reception/0/te: ‘Harp of the Spirit’ and ‘Sun of the Syrians’, the pre-eminent teacher of both East and West Syriac traditions.
fathers/ephrem-the-syrian/reception/1/te: Venerated on 28 January; known chiefly through the Greek Ephraem Graecus corpus and the Lenten prayer.
fathers/ephrem-the-syrian/reception/2/te: Declared a Doctor of the Church by Benedict XV in 1920 (encyclical Principi Apostolorum Petro); feast 9 June.
fathers/ephrem-the-syrian/reception/3/te: Commemorated (10 June in the Episcopal Church) as poet and teacher.
fathers/ephrem-the-syrian/controversies/: Authenticity: the large Greek, Armenian and Latin ‘Ephrem’ corpus is mostly not his
Legendary details of his life (pagan father, visit to Basil, refusal of priesthood by feigning madness)
His fierce anti-Jewish polemic in the Hymns on the Unleavened Bread and elsewhere
fathers/ephrem-the-syrian/quote/text: Lord, your symbols are everywhere, yet you are hidden from everywhere.
fathers/ephrem-the-syrian/places/2/name: Amida (Diyarbakır), region of exile from Nisibis
